A universal basic income (UBI) at any meaningful level is fiscally ruinous, economically distorting, and inferior to targeted alternatives. Providing even a modest $12,000 annually to every adult American would cost roughly $3 trillion per year before administrative overhead—on top of existing entitlements, defense, and interest on the national debt. That scale requires either confiscatory tax increases, monetization that produces inflation, or both. Historical analogs (Alaska's modest Permanent Fund dividend, Finland's limited trial, Stockton's small experiment) show modest well-being gains at tiny scale; they do not prove a national program works without collapsing labor participation or crowding out productive investment.

Work incentives matter.
